#### In this chapter
You will learn to use IJB, an Earth Engine application built by the author, by watching it work, step by step, on real places. First one landscape, Kota Besi in Kotawaringin Timur (Central Kalimantan), through every module: a clean image, the author's own 10-class land-cover model, canopy height learned from the GEDI laser, a per-village summary, plantation age, disturbance history and unsupervised clusters. Then four events: change around the new capital, the 2024 Demak flood, the 2023 peat fires in Ogan Komering Ilir and landslide susceptibility in West Java. Every map and number is the app's own result. No code is needed to use it; the rest of the book shows the code behind the same ideas.
:::

## Why an app

Most people who need a flood map are not programmers: a disaster officer, a district planner, a student on the first day. For them a script is a wall. IJB (from *Indraja Buana*, "remote sensing of the earth") puts the most useful analyses of this book behind buttons, with sensible defaults chosen from the author's own projects. It gives beginners real results on day one, and gives experts a fast first look before they open the Code Editor.

What you still need is the understanding from P1 to P5. The app will happily produce a flood map from the wrong dates or a land-cover map from three badly placed samples. Knowing *why* radar sees water and *what* an accuracy number means is what separates a usable result from a pretty one.

## Opening IJB

IJB is a published Earth Engine App, so it opens in an ordinary web browser.

1. Open <https://rifkynauvalhsp.users.earthengine.app/view/ijbexplorer> (short link: bit.ly/IJBExplorer).
2. Wait a few seconds while the frame loads: the panel on the left, the map on the right.
3. Start with Step 1 below.

The app loads only its frame at first. Each module is built the moment you press its button, so the app stays light, and if one module ever fails, its name and error appear on screen while the others keep working.

: Which module to open for which question.

The left panel walks you through three steps. The map on the right shows your area, every result layer, a legend and a status bar telling you what the app is doing.

### Step 1: area of interest

Every analysis needs an area. There are four ways to set it:

- **Draw** (*Gambar*) a rectangle (*Kotak*) or polygon (*Poligon*) on the map.
- **Choose an administrative unit** (*Wilayah*): *Pilih provinsi*, then *Pilih kabupaten atau kota*, from the official boundaries.
- **Paste** (*Tempel*) a geometry copied from QGIS, or four numbers of a bounding box (west, south, east, north).
- **Load a public Earth Engine asset** (*Aset*, then *Muat aset*), for example a boundary you uploaded yourself.

The app checks the size first and rejects areas over 25,000 km², because larger analyses would run out of time. A regency is usually well within the limit; a whole province often is not.

### Step 2: reporting unit

Choose whether statistics and tables are summarised per **province, regency, subdistrict (kecamatan) or village (desa)**. Subdistricts and villages use the official BPS boundaries (OCHA COD-AB, about 7,000 kecamatan and 82,000 desa). A flood map summarised per village is what an emergency response actually needs.

### Step 3: choose a module

Ten buttons, ten kinds of question. The table above says which to open for what. The rest of this chapter goes through them step by step, on real places, with the app's own results.

## How the results in this chapter were made

Every map, chart, table and number below was produced by the app itself, not redrawn by the book. Its modules were run headless: the Code Editor interface was replaced by a small harness (`tools/ijb_headless/harness.js`) that types the inputs a user would type and presses the module's own button, then saves the metric cards and the Earth Engine object behind every map layer. The maps below are those objects, computed again by Earth Engine and drawn with coordinates and a scale bar. To repeat a case yourself, open IJB, draw or choose the same area, enter the values in the first table and press the same button.

The full listing and every output are at the end of the chapter.

## Part A. One landscape, every module: Kota Besi

Kota Besi is a kecamatan of about 600 km² on the Mentaya river in Kotawaringin Timur, the oil palm heartland of Central Kalimantan. It has everything the modules are built for: plantations of different ages, rubber and sago smallholdings, river forest, peat and fire history. Each step below is one module: the clicks, then what the app returned. The table lists every input and every result card.

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-runs.qmd >}}

For every run, **Step 1** is *Wilayah* (Region): the kecamatan Kota Besi, and **Step 2** is *Satuan Pelaporan* (Reporting unit): *Desa*, so every table comes per village.

### Step A1. Citra: see the place first

![IJB Citra: the card before you press (left, buttons in red, in order) and what appears after (right).](images/real/p6-click-citra-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Citra: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Citra* · ② *Metode komposit*: *Cloud Score Plus (terbaik)* · ③ dates 1 June to 31 October 2024 (the dry season) · ④ *Kombinasi band*: *Warna alami* (natural colour) · ⑤ *Susun komposit*

**What the app returned:** *citra tersedia* (images available) **62**, *piksel bersih* (clear pixels) **99.6 %**.

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-citra.qmd >}}

Always look before you analyse. The river and its oxbows, the regular grid of plantation blocks in the north and south, and dark forest along the river are all visible. The five composite methods are explained in Chapter [-@sec-cloud]; Cloud Score+ is the best default in the tropics.

### Step A2. Model: the author's 10-class land-cover model

![IJB Model: the card before you press (left, buttons in red, in order) and what appears after (right).](images/real/p6-click-model-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Model: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Model* · ② *Mode*: *Model 10 kelas milik sendiri* · ③ *Tahun embedding* (embedding year): *2024* · ④ *Jalankan model*

**What the app returned:** *kelas dominan* (dominant class) **Kelapa Sawit** (oil palm), *luas kelas dominan* **21,109 ha**, with a pie chart of all classes and a CSV download.

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-model10.qmd >}}

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-model10-area.qmd >}}

This is the author's own classifier, trained in advance on 64 satellite-embedding bands plus elevation and slope, and stored as an Earth Engine asset. The app loads it and applies it to whatever area you choose, with no samples needed. Its classes are the ones that matter in Indonesian plantation landscapes: **oil palm, rubber and sago** are separate from **forest**, **agriculture** and **plantation** (other estate crops), with water, mangrove, rice field and open land. In Kota Besi, oil palm covers about a third of the kecamatan (35 %), followed by mixed agriculture (27 %), forest along the river (16 %), rubber (11 %) and sago (6 %).

**Why a local model matters.** Run the same module with *Mode*: *Dynamic World*, Google's global land-cover model, on the same area:

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-dw.qmd >}}

Dynamic World calls 54,742 ha, about nine tenths of Kota Besi, simply "trees". It is not wrong: palms, rubber and forest all have tree canopies. But it cannot say *which* trees, and that is exactly what a plantation agency, a buyer checking deforestation or a tax office needs. Splitting Dynamic World's "trees" with the 10-class model shows what is inside:

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-dw-vs-model10.qmd >}}

Of what the global model calls trees, the author's model finds 37 % oil palm, 26 % agriculture, 18 % forest, 11 % rubber and 6 % sago. A global map answers "is it green?"; a model trained on local classes answers "what is growing here?". That is the main reason to build your own model (Chapters [-@sec-supervised] and [-@sec-embeddings] show how), and the reason this app ships one.

### Step A3. Model: canopy height from the GEDI laser

**Clicks:** ① *Model* · ② *Mode*: *Tinggi tajuk dari GEDI* (canopy height from GEDI) · ③ GEDI dates 2019-04-01 to 2023-12-31 (default) · ④ *Tahun embedding*: *2024* · ⑤ *Jumlah pohon* (number of trees): 150 · ⑥ *Jalankan model*

**What the app returned:** *korelasi GEDI* (correlation with GEDI) **0.704**, *tinggi rerata* (mean height) **10.5 m**, the height map, a scatter chart, and downloads of the map and of mean height per desa.

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-chm.qmd >}}

GEDI, a laser on the International Space Station, measures canopy height only along narrow tracks of footprints 25 m wide (Chapter [-@sec-gedi-structure]). The app takes every good-quality footprint in your area (quality flag, no degradation, sensitivity above 0.95), keeps 70 % to train a random-forest regression on the embeddings, elevation and slope, and predicts height for every 10 m pixel. The other 30 % are kept aside to test it.

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read a scatter chart
A **scatter chart** puts one dot per observation on two axes. Here the horizontal axis is the height the laser *measured* at a test footprint, and the vertical axis is the height the model *predicted* there. If the model were perfect, every dot would sit on the dashed **1:1 line**.

Read it in three steps:

1. **How tight is the cloud around the line?** That is the correlation (*r*) and the typical error (RMSE, in metres).
2. **Is the cloud tilted less than the 1:1 line?** The fitted red line has a slope of about 0.5: the model **under-predicts tall canopies and over-predicts short ones**. This is normal for a regression, which pulls predictions towards the average, and it means the map compresses the range: the tallest forest is lower on the map than in reality.
3. **Are there dots far from the rest?** Those are footprints on a forest edge, a gap or a cloud, worth checking before trusting the map there.
:::

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-scatter.qmd >}}

On 400 test footprints the correlation is 0.76 with an RMSE of 3.9 m, and the slope of 0.54 shows the compression. For a landscape of oil palm (10–15 m) and young regrowth it is a good map; for estimating the height of the tallest forest it would need tall-canopy training data or a dedicated height product (Chapter [-@sec-height-scaling]).

### Step A4. Toolbox: chain one result into the next

Every result becomes the *lapisan aktif* (active layer), and every tool in the Toolbox works on the active layer. So, right after the height map:

**Clicks:** ① *Toolbox* · ② *Alat* (Tool): *Statistik zonal* (zonal statistics) · ③ *Statistik*: *Rerata* (mean) · ④ *Jalankan operasi*

**What the app returned:** *hasil* **24 wilayah** (24 villages), with a chart and a CSV of mean canopy height per desa.

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-desa.qmd >}}

That is a table a district forestry office can use directly: Kota Besi Hilir, with its river forest, has the tallest canopy (14.5 m mean). The other tools chain the same way: threshold, vectorise, segment, filter, buffer, contour (the figure below).

![Chaining tools: every result becomes the active layer for the next one.](images/real/p6-chain-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="Chaining tools: every result becomes the active layer for the next one."}

### Step A5. Deret: how old, and when did it change?

![IJB Deret: the card before you press (left, buttons in red, in order) and what appears after (right).](images/real/p6-click-deret-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Deret: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks for age:** ① *Deret* · ② *Mode*: *Umur tegakan atau tanaman* (stand or crop age) · ③ *Rentang tahun*: 1990 to 2024 · ④ *Jalankan analisis*

**What the app returned:** *umur rerata* (mean age) **17.6 years**, over **33,372 ha** with a clear regrowth segment.

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-age.qmd >}}

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-age-years.qmd >}}

The app builds an annual Landsat NBR series, runs LandTrendr, and dates the start of the largest growth segment: the year a block was planted or a forest regrew (the same idea as Chapter [-@sec-oil-palm-age], where the GEDI test showed which dates to trust). The distribution of planting years is what a replanting plan starts from. In Kota Besi most stands began between 2007 and 2016, peaking in 2012–2013, so most of the planted area is now 10–19 years old, in its prime. The spike at 1998 is the 1997–98 El Niño: regrowth after the great fires, or the haze-year dates that Chapter [-@sec-oil-palm-age] warned about. Those pixels need checking before anyone plans replanting from them.

**Clicks for disturbance:** the same, with *Mode*: *Titik patah LandTrendr* and years 2000 to 2024.

**What the app returned:** *tahun gangguan dominan* (main disturbance year) **2012**, *luas terganggu* (area disturbed) **30,460 ha**.

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-disturb.qmd >}}

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-disturb-years.qmd >}}

The year of the largest drop in NBR marks clearing, fire or replanting. Read the chart with the age map. Clearing peaked in 2010–2012, just before the planting wave of 2011–2013: that is the plantation expansion, cleared and planted within a year or two. Since 2016 little new land has been disturbed. The tall bar at 2000 is partly an edge effect: the first year of the series also collects change from before it. Disturbance with no regrowth after it is a loss worth investigating.

### Step A6. Tutupan: your own classes

![IJB Tutupan: the card before you press (left, buttons in red, in order) and what appears after (right).](images/real/p6-click-tutupan-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Tutupan: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks (no samples):** ① *Tutupan* · ② *Sumber data*: *Sentinel-2 komposit*, dates 2024 · ③ *Algoritma*: *K-Means* · ④ *Latih dan klasifikasi*

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p6-kmeans.qmd >}}

K-Means needs no samples: it groups pixels that look alike into six clusters, and you decide what each cluster is by looking at the image. It is the fastest way to see the structure of a place. For a map you can report, switch *Algoritma* to *Random Forest*, press *Tambah* (Add) for each class, press *Tandai* (Mark) and click examples on the map, then *Latih dan klasifikasi*. The app then reports overall accuracy and kappa and the area of every class (Chapters [-@sec-supervised] and [-@sec-accuracy]); spread your samples over the whole area, because accuracy on points clicked close together is optimistic.

### Step A7. Data: the catalogue behind everything

![IJB Data: the card before you press (left, buttons in red, in order) and what appears after (right).](images/real/p6-click-data-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Data: before and after pressing the button."}

**Clicks:** ① *Wilayah* (Region): choose province and regency · ② *Data* · ③ *Kelompok* (Group): *Curah hujan* · ④ *Lapisan* (Layer) · ⑤ *Rentang tanggal* (Date range) · ⑥ *Tampilkan lapisan* (Show layer)

**After you press:** the result cards show *rerata di AOI* (mean over the area) and *jenis* (type); the map shows the result layer.


Forty-three ready datasets in thirteen groups: hydrology, rainfall, terrain, land cover, buildings and population, fire and peat, drought, coasts and ecosystems, soils, volcanoes, administrative boundaries, event history and machine learning. Examples: CHIRPS and GPM rainfall, HAND and MERIT Hydro, four elevation models (FABDEM, Copernicus GLO-30, NASADEM, SRTM), Dynamic World and WorldCover, Google, Microsoft and VIDA building footprints, WorldPop and GHSL population, FIRMS hotspots, burned area, peat extent and peat thickness, mangroves, SMAP soil moisture, the NASA global landslide catalogue and the satellite embeddings. Pick a group and a layer, set a date range where relevant, and press *Tampilkan lapisan*: the layer appears on the map with its mean over your area.

**Use it for:** a first look at any place, and background layers before any analysis.

## Part B. Four events, four modules

The second half uses the event modules where they matter most, on four real cases.

### Ubah: change around the new capital, Penajam Paser Utara, 2019 to 2024

![IJB Ubah: the card before you press (left, buttons in red, in order) and what appears after (right).](images/real/p6-click-ubah-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Ubah: before and after pressing the button."}

Penajam Paser Utara holds the core of Nusantara, Indonesia's new capital. The Ubah module subtracts the NDVI of a cloud-free 2019 composite from that of 2024 and calls a change real above ±0.2.

The app reports **10,923 ha greener-to-browner** and **18,907 ha browner-to-greener**. The map shows where. The tight red pattern of roads and cleared ground in the north around 116.7° E, 0.95° S is the capital's core zone (compare the time-lapse in Chapter [-@sec-visualisation]); the large rectangular green and red blocks across the regency are plantation forestry, harvested in one period and replanted in the other. More greening than browning in a region famous for clearing is not a contradiction: an NDVI difference records plantation regrowth as gain, which is why Chapter [-@sec-eudr] separates forest from tree crops before calling anything deforestation.

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p7-ubah-ppu.qmd >}}

### Banjir: the Demak flood, March 2024

![IJB Banjir: the card before you press (left, buttons in red, in order) and what appears after (right).](images/real/p6-click-banjir-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Banjir: before and after pressing the button."}

In mid-March 2024, river embankments failed in Demak, Central Java, and floodwater spread across rice fields and villages for weeks. The Banjir module compares a Sentinel-1 image before the event with one after it, finds the backscatter drop that marks open water with an automatic (Otsu) threshold, then removes steep ground, permanent water and land high above the drainage network.

With the app's defaults and the event dates, it maps **2,341 ha** of new flooding, with about **29,000 people** living in the flooded cells (WorldPop) and 49 mapped buildings hit. Two facts belong next to those numbers. The only descending Sentinel-1 pass in the window is 15 March, early in the event, so this is a snapshot of the first days, not the maximum extent. And a large part of the district appears black in both images: fishponds and paddies already under water in February, which a change-based method cannot count as new flooding by design. The "overlap with past floods" card (35 %) compares the result with the Global Flood Database of 2000-2018 events; a low overlap is expected for a flood caused by a levee breach rather than by the usual rainfall pattern.

A district total is not what a disaster office works with. Set the reporting level to **Kecamatan** and the same run gives the exposure table per subdistrict, which the app draws as a chart and offers as a CSV. In Demak, two kecamatan carry most of the flood: **Karang Tengah** (about 1,080 ha flooded, 10,500 people in the flooded cells) and **Bonang** (700 ha, 5,600 people), followed by Sayung, Karanganyar and Wedung. The southern kecamatan, such as Karangawen, show no new water. The boundaries are the official BPS subdistricts, distributed by OCHA, so the names match those on a BPBD situation report.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A habit worth copying from the app: give a mosaic a projection
The app loads terrain models (FABDEM, Copernicus GLO-30, ALOS AW3D30) as a `mosaic()` of tiles. An Earth Engine mosaic has no native projection: its default grid is one degree, about 111 km. Run `ee.Terrain.slope()` on it unchanged, and the slope is computed on 111 km cells, so a slope mask removes nothing or everything. The app therefore gives each mosaic the projection of its first tile before any terrain operation. Do the same in your own scripts: `.setDefaultProjection(c.first().select(0).projection())`. More generally, **when a result is exactly zero, check the pipeline before reporting it.**
:::

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p7-banjir-demak.qmd >}}

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p7-banjir-kecamatan.qmd >}}

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p7-banjir-kecamatan-table.qmd >}}

### Api: the 2023 fire season on the peat of Ogan Komering Ilir

![IJB Api: the card before you press (left, buttons in red, in order) and what appears after (right).](images/real/p6-click-api-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Api: before and after pressing the button."}

Ogan Komering Ilir in South Sumatra is mostly peat, and 2023 was an El Niño year. The Api module maps burn severity from the change in the normalised burn ratio between Sentinel-2 composites before and after the season, counts FIRMS hotspots, and overlays global peat extent and thickness.

The app reports **290,030 ha** in the burn-severity classes and **3,817 hotspots**, and of the burned area, **238,586 ha lies on peat**, with a mean modelled peat depth of **151 cm** under it. That last pair is the point of the module: a hectare of burned peat 1.5 m deep is a very different carbon and health event from a hectare of burned grass.

Read the map before the numbers. The post-fire Sentinel-2 composite has whole swaths missing between about 2.8° and 3.6° S, where cloud and haze left no clear observation, so the burned area covers only part of the district; the true figure is higher in that sense. In the other direction, the lowest severity class also catches non-fire change such as harvest and seasonal browning. The 290,030 ha is therefore a screening number for the covered area, to be checked against a burned-area product such as MODIS MCD64A1 (Chapter [-@sec-peat]) before it goes into a report.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why a card can show "—"
Some districts are too large for one Earth Engine request, so the app computes areas in tiles (`tileScale`). If a value still cannot be computed, the card shows "—" rather than 0. A missing value must never look like a measured one: "0 ha of burned peat" is a finding, "—" is an honest "not computed". Build the same rule into your own tools.
:::

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p7-api-oki.qmd >}}

### Rawan: landslide susceptibility across West Java

![IJB Rawan: the card before you press (left, buttons in red, in order) and what appears after (right).](images/real/p6-click-rawan-en.png){.lightbox fig-alt="IJB Rawan: before and after pressing the button."}

The Rawan module trains a random forest on satellite embeddings, terrain, rainfall, soil and land cover, using either points the user places or, automatically, events from the NASA Global Landslide Catalog. In automatic mode the module first counts the catalogue landslides in the area and needs **at least 20**. For Kabupaten Bandung Barat the catalogue holds only 9, so the app asks the user to widen the area or place points by hand. The rule exists for a reason worth understanding. Nine landslides against 200 random "safe" points would let a random forest call everything safe and still score 92 % accuracy, because 92 % is simply the share of safe points. That model would have a kappa of zero and map no hazard at all. When classes are this unbalanced, read kappa, not accuracy.

Across the whole province there are enough events. The app reports **81.3 % validation accuracy and a kappa of 0.38**, with 12,482 ha of high susceptibility.

Now look at the map. The highest values are in the Bandung basin and around Bogor, densely built and largely flat, while the steep, wet southern mountains look comparatively safe. This comes from the training data, not from the method. A catalogue compiled from news reports records landslides where people live and roads run, so a model trained on it learns "near towns and roads" as much as "steep, wet, weak slopes". The same bias inflates the "people in susceptible zones" card. Use the automatic mode only to see the method work; for a susceptibility map that will inform planning, place points from a field inventory or a polygon inventory mapped from imagery (Chapter [-@sec-landslide-simple] shows why the news-based catalogue fails as a test set), and check that slope and rainfall, not land cover, carry the model.

{{< include _snippets/ch00g_ijb_cases__p7-rawan-jabar.qmd >}}

## Four recipes

**A flood situation report.** Step 1: choose the regency. Step 2: reporting unit *Desa*. Banjir: before period a month before the event, after period the days just after it, the orbit that passed during the flood. Run. Read hectares, people and buildings per village; check the map against news photographs before sharing it.

**A burn-severity map for a peat district.** Api with a before period in June–July and an after period in October–November of a dry year. Read the burned peat and its thickness; use Data → FIRMS to compare with hotspot counts.

**Urban growth.** Ubah with *Dynamic World transitions* between two years, or *Selisih indeks* on NDBI. For building counts, Data → VIDA building footprints, then Toolbox → zonal statistics per village.

**A quick land-cover map with no samples.** Model → the 10-class model for the latest embedding year. If your area has classes the model never saw, switch to Tutupan and train your own.

## Reading app results critically

Every case above produced a tidy card with a plausible number. The work was in deciding what each number can bear. Three habits did that work, and they apply to any tool, your own scripts included:

1. **Run it on cases where you know roughly what the answer should be.** A famous flood, a peat district, a construction site.
2. **Treat exactly zero, exactly 100 % and a perfect-looking accuracy as questions, not answers.**
3. **Look at the map before the metric.** The ponds already under water in Demak, the cloud gaps in the fire composite and the urban hotspot in the susceptibility map were all visible before any number was read.

## Using an app responsibly

- **Dates are everything.** A flood map from the wrong week maps rice-field irrigation (Chapter [-@sec-paddy]).
- **Read the numbers the app gives you,** especially accuracy and kappa, and treat any map without them as a draft.
- **Check against something independent**: field reports, high-resolution basemaps, news photographs.
- **Credit the data.** Every layer in the catalogue has an owner; name them when you publish a map.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Run Model → *Model 10 kelas milik sendiri* for your own kabupaten, then *Dynamic World* for the same area. Which of the 10 classes does Dynamic World merge, and does it matter for your question?
2. Run Model → canopy height for a forest area. Read the scatter chart: what is the slope of the cloud, and which canopies does the map under-estimate?
3. After the height map, use Toolbox → *Statistik zonal* per desa. Which village has the tallest canopy, and what is there on the 10-class map?
4. Run Deret → age for a plantation district. When were most blocks planted, and how many hectares will reach 25 years in the next five?
5. Map a flood you know with Banjir, reporting per *Kecamatan*. Which orbit direction passed closest to the event date?
6. Use Rawan with points you place by hand on mapped landslides from a published inventory. Does the hotspot in the Bandung basin remain?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** It depends on your kabupaten. Dynamic World has nine global classes, so the author's plantation classes, oil palm, rubber and sago, all fall into its single "trees" class, together with forest; in Kota Besi that was 54,742 ha, about nine tenths of the area. If your question is forest against non-forest, Dynamic World may be enough; if it is which crop, who owns the trees, or deforestation by commodity, the merge matters and the 10-class model is the one to use.

**2.** In Kota Besi the fitted line has a slope of about 0.5 (0.54 on 400 test footprints, r 0.76, RMSE 3.9 m). Your area will differ, but expect a slope below 1: the regression pulls predictions towards the average, so it under-estimates the tallest canopies and over-estimates short ones. Tall, old forest is lower on the map than in reality, which matters most for carbon.

**3.** Not computed in the chapter; it depends on your area. Expect the tallest village mean where the 10-class map shows the most forest or old, tall plantations; a village dominated by oil palm will sit around 10-15 m. Compare the village's height with its class mix: if a village is tall but the map shows mostly plantation, check the classes there before trusting either.

**4.** Not computed in the chapter; it depends on the district. Read the planting-year histogram: most plantation districts show one or two waves of planting, for example a boom in the 2000s. Blocks reach 25 years, the usual replanting age, five years after the planting year passes the current year minus 25; sum the hectares planted in the window (current year − 30) to (current year − 25) to get the area due for replanting in the next five years.

**5.** Not computed in the chapter; it depends on the flood. Sentinel-1 passes the same place on ascending and descending orbits at different days and times; check the acquisition dates the module lists and choose the orbit whose after-image is closest to the peak of the flood, ideally within a day or two. A pass several days later shows only the water that remained, so the flood area will be smaller.

**6.** Not computed in the chapter. With points placed on mapped landslides from a published inventory, which covers the steep, wet southern mountains as well as places near roads and towns, the training data no longer follow where news reports come from. Expect the Bandung basin hotspot to weaken or disappear and the southern mountains to rise, which shows that the earlier hotspot came from the catalogue's reporting bias, not from the terrain.
:::
